title: Measuring Verifier Impact in an LLM Generate→Verify→Repair Loop for Intent→Configuration NetOps Tasks
abstract: We measure how inserting a deterministic network verifier into a generate→verify→repair loop changes verifier-detected safety violations of LLM-produced device-configuration proposals. In a preregistered paired design (N = 500 deterministic intent→configuration tasks stratified across VLAN-change, ACL-change, and static-route-change clusters) we compared: (1) baseline — a single LLM proposal (requested model: gpt-5-mini) produced once per task, and (2) guarded — the identical shared proposal examined by a deterministic netops validator with up to one automated repair iteration invoked only if the validator flagged a preregistered high/medium-severity violation. Primary outcome: verifier pass (no preregistered high/medium-severity violations). Results (complete pairs = 500): baseline passed 499/500 (0.998), guarded passed 500/500 (1.000); contingency: n11 = 499, n10 = 1, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. Absolute paired success-rate difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.002. The archived analysis used an exact McNemar two-sided convention implemented as an exact binomial on discordant pairs (n = n10 + n01), producing two-sided p = 1.00 for the observed single discordant pair; paired-bootstrap percentile 95% CI = [0.0, 0.006] (B = 10,000, seed = 1729). Interpretation: on this verifier-scoped synthetic corpus and model+validator pairing the LLM produced near-ceiling proposals; the marginal numeric verifier+repair effect on the pass-rate metric is therefore small, though the verifier+repair loop deterministically corrected one concrete baseline failure (repair-stage calls observed = 1). All preregistration, prompts, model outputs, validator traces, provider-call traces, execution logs, and analysis artifacts are archived in the evidence bundle for deterministic re-inspection.

sections.introduction:
Motivation. Large language models (LLMs) are being integrated into NetOps/AIOps workflows to translate operator intent into device configurations, plan multi-step changes, and propose repairs. Systems and surveys emphasize that operational safety typically depends on surrounding engineering—deterministic validators, sandbox replay, canarying, and rollback—rather than on the model alone [https://doi.org/10.1145/3098822.3098834; https://doi.org/10.1145/3718958.3750537; https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2605.12729]. A common architectural pattern is generate→verify→repair (G→V→R): the model generates a candidate; a deterministic verifier checks formalized properties; and automated or human repairs are applied when violations appear.

Research question and contribution. Despite conceptual agreement about guards, there is limited controlled, artifact-backed measurement isolating the verifier’s marginal contribution when the model’s initial proposal is held fixed. We therefore preregistered and executed a confirmatory paired experiment that answers: How much does integrating a deterministic verifier plus one automated repair iteration reduce verifier-detected safety violations in LLM-generated proposals when the initial proposal is identical across arms? Our contributions are: (1) a preregistered paired study (N = 500) with deterministic task generation and archived artifacts; (2) a precise statistical report (exact paired McNemar convention, paired-bootstrap CIs) and execution accounting (model_calls_used = 501, repair-stage calls = 1); (3) an operational interpretation highlighting ceiling effects, design-semantic tradeoffs (shared_initial_candidate vs verifier-guided regeneration), and artifact-grounded reproducibility guidance.
sections.related_work:
Deterministic verification and generate–verify patterns. Formal and deterministic verification techniques for network configurations (header-space analysis, route-model verifiers) can detect reachability and safety violations and are foundational to NetOps verification literature [https://doi.org/10.1145/3098822.3098834]. Contemporary NetOps/AIOps works and system reports show LLM-based intent translators and stress the need for validators and guardrails to reach operational reliability (INTA, Confucius, and recent reviews) [https://doi.org/10.1109/icnp65844.2025.11192391; https://doi.org/10.1145/3718958.3750537; https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.12729]. Generate→verify→repair appears across structured-generation domains as a practical method to reduce incorrect outputs; however, published instantiations seldom provide controlled ablations that quantify the verifier’s marginal effect under reproducible conditions.

Failure-mode and evaluation gaps. Prior studies document LLM failure modes (hallucination, overconfidence, inconsistent CLIs), motivating guardrails and human oversight [doi:10.2139/ssrn.6484501; arXiv:2309.05557]. Surveys highlight the lack of standardized safety-centric NetOps benchmarks that measure operational outcomes (e.g., MTTR, rollback success) rather than task accuracy alone; this motivated our verifier-scoped synthetic benchmark design [https://doi.org/10.1145/3641289]. Our work complements prior systems by making a narrowly scoped, preregistered measurement with full artifact archiving.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and confirmatory plan. The full preregistration (study_id cand_7f4b9a2d_hosted_gvr_v1_2026) froze the research question, inclusion/exclusion rules, task-generation seeds, estimands, multiplicity plan, retry policy, and stopping rule before data collection. Primary confirmatory hypothesis: an LLM paired with a deterministic verifier plus a single automated repair iteration will produce a lower verifier-detected safety-violation rate than the same LLM producing a single proposal without verifier feedback (paired within-task). Primary estimand: paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline where success == verifier reports zero preregistered high/medium-severity violations. The preregistration SHA-256 is archived in the execution manifest and recorded in the evidence bundle.

Task generation and constraints. We generated a deterministic synthetic corpus of 500 intent→configuration tasks using deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5 with preregistered seeds and stratified allocation: VLAN-change (167), ACL-change (167), static-route-change (166). Task payloads constrained allowed_fields to {admin, mtu, vlan} to match the verifier’s modeled coverage; tasks referencing unmodeled features would have been excluded per preregistration (no such exclusions occurred). Each task contains initial_state, expected_final_state, and an explicit required_sequence; representative task manifests and examples are archived under execution/task_manifest.jsonl and the representative_tasks entries in the bundle.

Generation semantics and experimental control. To isolate verifier+repair marginal effect conditional on identical proposals we used generation_semantics = "shared_initial_candidate" with independent_condition_generation = false. For each task the pipeline produced a single shared LLM candidate (requested model: gpt-5-mini). The baseline arm recorded that shared response as the model-only proposal; the guarded arm validated the identical shared candidate and invoked the single automated repair iteration only if the verifier reported a preregistered high/medium-severity violation. This design was preregistered and intentionally avoids conflation with verifier-guided regeneration or independent guarded-generation strategies.

Model and validator. The requested LLM is gpt-5-mini called through the hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter (provider recorded as openai_responses); model_configuration.json (archived) records max_output_tokens = 2000 and single-attempt generation semantics. The deterministic validator used for gating and scoring is deterministic_netops_validator_v5; its property coverage and the violation-code→severity mapping are archived in validator-spec artifacts in the evidence bundle. The guarded arm allowed at most one automated repair iteration per the preregistered contract.

Primary test: exact McNemar (archived implementation). The preregistered confirmatory test is an exact McNemar two-sided test on paired binary outcomes. Our archived analysis executor implements the standard exact-pair approach via the discordant-pair binomial: let n = n10 + n01 (discordant pairs) and let X be Binomial(n, 0.5). The two-sided p-value is computed as p_two-sided = 2 × min{P(X ≤ n10), P(X ≥ n10)}, truncated at 1.0. For small n this exact binomial two-sided rule is the conventional exact McNemar implementation used by our executor; the executor’s parameters and code are archived in analysis/analysis_log.jsonl. For the observed discordant counts (n10 = 1, n01 = 0, therefore n = 1) both tail probabilities equal 0.5 and the two-sided p becomes 2 × 0.5 = 1.0; we therefore report two-sided p = 1.00 and explain its practical implication in Results.

Bootstrap confidence intervals. We computed paired-bootstrap percentile 95% CIs for the absolute success-rate difference using B = 10,000 resamples (bootstrap_seed = 1729). The resampling unit preserves pairs (each resample draws 500 pairs with replacement). Bootstrap code, seed, and resampling semantics are archived under analysis/ and analysis_log.jsonl.

Missingness, retries, and stopping rule. The preregistered retry policy allowed up to two automated retries for transient model-provider errors. The run stopped when the preregistered confirmatory pairs (N = 500) completed. The execution manifest records model_calls_used = 501, completed_episode_count = 1000, failed_episode_count = 0, and observed repair-stage calls = 1. All raw provider-call traces, response texts, validator traces, and retry metadata are archived in the evidence bundle and deterministically retrievable.
sections.results:
Primary counts and contingency table. The study completed with complete_pair_count = 500 and model_calls_used = 501 (shared_initial_generation = 500 and repair-stage calls = 1). Aggregated per-condition counts (analysis/condition_summary.csv): baseline successes = 499, baseline failures = 1 (baseline_success_rate = 0.998); guarded successes = 500, guarded failures = 0 (guarded_success_rate = 1.000). The paired contingency table (guarded × baseline, analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv) is: n11 = 499, n10 = 1, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. Absolute paired success-rate difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.002.

Exact McNemar two-sided p and interpretation. Applying the archived exact-McNemar implementation on discordant pairs (n = n10 + n01 = 1) yields two-sided p = 1.00 for the observed n10 = 1, n01 = 0. The numeric p = 1.00 arises from the two-sided binomial rule (p_two-sided = 2 × min{P(X ≤ 1), P(X ≥ 1)} with X ∼ Binomial(1, 0.5)). This formal p-value reflects extremely low discordant-pair counts (n small) rather than evidence that the guarded arm is harmful; inferential power is weak under such a ceiling regime. We therefore emphasize effect-size reporting and paired-bootstrap CIs: paired-bootstrap percentile 95% CI for the absolute difference = [0.0, 0.006] (B = 10,000, seed = 1729).

Repair activity and discordant-pair provenance. Observed repair-stage provider calls = 1; that single repair produced the sole discordant outcome (n10 = 1) — the guarded arm converted one baseline-detected violation into a verified pass. The execution archive contains the complete per-task validator diagnostics, normalized configurations, repair prompt/response, and provider-call trace for that episode. The discordant episode is deterministically locatable in the archived execution/raw_results.jsonl by filtering for pairs where baseline scoring indicates a preregistered high/medium-severity violation (baseline pass == 0) while guarded scoring indicates pass == 1; because exactly one such pair exists the filter returns the single episode and its repair-stage provider-call trace. The evidence bundle therefore substantiates the concrete corrective event even though the aggregated numeric gain is small.

Secondary analyses and ceiling effect. The preregistered per-violation-class secondary analyses were uninformative because observed violation counts were nearly zero; there were no meaningful counts to support class-level inference. The preregistration assumed a higher baseline error prevalence (used for power planning, target p_b ≈ 0.30); the observed prevalence (0.002 failure rate) created a ceiling effect that substantially reduced power to detect small absolute gains on the pass-rate metric. Analysis artifacts include missingness_summary.csv and contamination_summary.csv; both indicate no exclusions, no missing pairs, and no contamination events in this run. All numeric tables and logs are archived under analysis/ and execution/ paths similarly recorded in the manifest.
sections.discussion:
Operational interpretation. Under the preregistered constrained regime (requested LLM = gpt-5-mini, shared_initial_candidate semantics, deterministic_netops_validator_v5 with allowed_fields = {admin, mtu, vlan}, and a single permitted repair iteration) the LLM produced near-ceiling correct proposals; consequently, the measured absolute verifier+repair benefit on the composite pass-rate metric is small (0.002). This should not be taken to mean verifiers are unnecessary: the verifier corrected one concrete baseline failure, demonstrating corrective potential. In production workloads with higher baseline error prevalence, broader verifier coverage, or heterogeneous vendor CLIs, verifier+repair gains could be substantially larger.

Design-semantic tradeoffs. The shared_initial_candidate semantics intentionally isolate verifier+repair impact conditional on identical proposals. That choice answers a narrowly operational question: how much additional safety does a verifier+single-repair provide when the model’s proposed change is fixed? Alternative operational semantics (verifier-guided regeneration, unrestricted multiple repairs, or independent guarded generation) address different deployment priorities (cost of model calls, final-pass probability irrespective of regeneration cost, or minimizing human review). Practitioners must match generation semantics in experiments to the operational decision they intend to inform.

Threats to validity. Internal validity: supported by preregistered paired design, deterministic seeds, and automated exclusion rules (no manual adjudication), but power assumptions failed due to unexpectedly low baseline error prevalence. Construct validity: the pass/fail outcome is defined relative to the verifier’s modeled property set and severity mapping (archived); properties outside that mapping are not assessed. External validity: single model family and single validator on a synthetic corpus limit cross-vendor and multi-model generalization. Conclusion validity: small discordant counts (n = 1) lead to weak inferential power for the exact test and motivate emphasis on effect-size reporting and archived per-episode audit.

Operational recommendations. (1) Measure baseline proposal error prevalence on representative operational data before investing in expensive automated-repair budgets: when baseline error is already extremely low, marginal pass-rate gains from verifier+repair pipelines on the pass-rate metric may be small. (2) Ensure verifier property coverage aligns with operator-critical constraints; validator-spec artifacts in the bundle document the mapping used here. (3) Select generation semantics that match deployment goals: shared_initial_candidate isolates marginal corrective power; verifier-guided regeneration may yield larger final-pass rates at the cost of additional model calls and complexity. The evidence bundle includes exemplar repair traces and logs to evaluate repair costs and latencies.
sections.conclusion: We executed a preregistered, artifact-backed paired experiment (N = 500) isolating the verifier+single-repair effect under shared_initial_candidate semantics. Results show a very small absolute improvement in this constrained regime (guarded 500/500 vs baseline 499/500; absolute difference 0.002; paired-bootstrap 95% CI [0.0, 0.006]; archived exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.00 under the executor’s two-sided binomial convention). The outcome illustrates a ceiling-effect regime in which near-perfect model proposals limit measurable verifier benefits on the pass-rate metric, yet the verifier still corrected at least one concrete failure. Operators should align task semantics, verifier coverage, and measurement metrics with operational priorities; the archived evidence bundle deterministically supports all claims and enables follow-up ablations (e.g., verifier-guided regeneration or larger repair budgets) without manual reconstruction of the run.

limitations: Synthetic, deterministic task corpus limited to features modeled by the deterministic validator; the task payloads in the archive show allowed_fields = {admin, mtu, vlan}. Results do not necessarily generalize to unconstrained production intents, cross-vendor CLI heterogeneity, or protocol semantics outside the verifier scope.
Single model family tested (gpt-5-mini requested) and a single validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) — no claim of multi-model generality is made.
Maximum one automated repair iteration was permitted by the preregistration; different repair budgets or iterative regeneration strategies could change measured verifier impact.

Very high baseline pass rate (499/500) created a ceiling effect that limits power to detect small absolute improvements on the pass-rate metric; the archived exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.00 must be interpreted in that context and reflects the archived two-sided exact-binomial convention for n = 1 discordant pair.

The single discordant episode (the sole task where baseline failed and guarded succeeded) and its validator diagnostics and repair-stage trace are archived in execution/raw_results.jsonl in the evidence bundle. To inspect it deterministically: filter execution/raw_results.jsonl for pair_id entries where the baseline scoring outcome indicates a preregistered high/medium-severity violation (baseline pass == 0) while the guarded scoring outcome indicates pass == 1; because only one such discordant pair exists in the confirmatory set, this lookup returns the single episode and its provider-call traces. The validator violation-code→severity mapping is archived in the execution manifest and validator-spec artifacts in the bundle.
